author: Recurse

lesson.intro: Knowing networking is most of passing the CCNA, but not all of it. This lesson covers how the 200-301 exam works, how to spend its 120 minutes, how to read exhibits and eliminate wrong answers, how booking, retakes and recertification work, and a 12-week plan that uses the CCNA path, its labs, daily review and practice exams. Anything Cisco can change, such as the price or the policies, is marked so you check the current details on cisco.com.
objectives: Describe the 200-301 exam's format, item types and the rule that you cannot go back
Plan a time budget and a reading routine for exhibit and multiple-answer items
Book the exam through Pearson VUE at a test center or online and follow the rules for each
Follow a 12-week plan and a final-week routine that end with steady practice exam scores

sections.title: What the 200-301 exam is
sections.body:
One exam, 200-301 CCNA (Implementing and Administering Cisco Solutions), earns the certification. There are no prerequisites. Some facts Cisco publishes; others it deliberately does not, and you should know which is which.

Published by Cisco (verified on cisco.com in October 2026; check the current details on cisco.com before you book):

- **Duration:** 120 minutes.
- **Price:** USD 300 plus tax. That was also the price when the Official Cert Guide was printed. Local prices and currencies vary, and you can pay with a voucher or Cisco Learning Credits.
- **Languages:** English and Japanese.
- **Delivery:** Pearson VUE, at a test center or online with a live remote proctor (OnVUE).
- **Exam topics and weights:** Network Fundamentals 20%, Network Access 20%, IP Connectivity 25%, IP Services 10%, Security Fundamentals 15%, Automation and Programmability 10%. The CCNA path in Recurse follows these six domains in this order.

Not published:

- **The number of questions.** Candidates commonly report roughly 100 items, give or take. Treat that as unofficial: you learn your own count only when the exam starts.
- **The passing score.** Cisco says passing scores are set by statistical analysis and can change without notice, so it does not publish them. Unofficial reports usually put the mark somewhere around 800 to 850 out of 1000. Do not plan around a number; plan to clear it comfortably. Recurse's practice exams use 85% as the bar for booking.

The verbs in the exam topics tell you how deep to go. Describe, explain and compare topics need concepts. Configure, verify and troubleshoot topics also need commands and the ability to read show output, which is where most of the time pressure comes from. Cisco also states that the exam may include related topics that are not listed, so learn the neighborhood of each item, not just its exact wording.

sections.tip: Book the exam when your timed practice exam scores are steady at 85% or more, not on the day you finish the last lesson.
sections.pitfall: Treating an unofficial passing score as the target. Cisco does not publish it and it can change, so aim well above any number you read online.

check.question: Which statement about the CCNA 200-301 passing score is accurate?
choices: It is fixed at 825 out of 1000
It is 70% of the questions answered correctly

It is printed on the exam topics page
check.explanation: Cisco's exam policies say passing scores are set by statistical analysis, are subject to change and are not published. Figures such as 825 are unofficial reports.

sections.title: Item types and the one-way rule
sections.body:
Expect these item types. Cisco does not say how many of each you will get.

- **Multiple choice, single answer:** round radio buttons, one choice.
- **Multiple choice, multiple answer:** square check boxes, and the question says how many to pick ("Choose two"). The software stops you choosing too many and warns you if you choose too few.
- **Drag and drop:** match items to categories or put steps in order. You can rearrange freely until you move on. Recurse's match and order questions train exactly this.
- **Testlet:** one scenario with several multiple-choice questions.
- **Simlet:** a simulated network you explore with show commands, plus several multiple-choice questions about its current state. You may be limited to user EXEC mode.
- **Simulation (sim):** a simulated network where you configure or fix something. You are graded on the result.

The rule that changes everything: **you cannot go back.** Once you click Next, that item is locked. There is no review screen at the end and no flagging. Inside a testlet or simlet you can move between its tabs, but the Next button that leaves the scenario does not warn you that a tab is unanswered or has too few answers selected. Check every tab before you leave.

There is no penalty for guessing, so never leave anything blank. If you are stuck, eliminate what you can, choose the best remaining answer and move on. You cannot come back to it, so there is nothing to gain by hesitating.

Before exam day, watch Cisco's exam tutorial videos on the Cisco Learning Network so the simulator window, the topology toggle and the scroll bars are familiar. In simulations you usually reach a device's console by clicking the PC attached to it (the console cable is drawn as a dashed line). Read the whole task, including anything in a scroll area, before typing.
sections.code:
Item type        Time each    Can change answer?
Single answer    about 1 min  until you click Next
Multiple answer  about 1 min  until you click Next
Drag and drop    about 1 min  until you click Next
Testlet          6 to 8 min   between its tabs
Simlet           6 to 8 min   between its tabs
Simulation       6 to 8 min   until you click Next
sections.tip: In Recurse exams, answer in order and do not use Back or Flag. Practicing the one-way flow builds the habit you need on the real exam.
sections.pitfall: Clicking Next out of a simlet after answering three of its four tabs. The exam only asks whether you want to move on; it does not tell you a tab is still blank.

check.question: You are unsure about a single-answer question and have ruled out two choices. What should you do?
choices: Skip it and come back at the end
Pick the better of the remaining two and move on
Leave it blank to avoid losing points for a wrong answer
Flag it for the review screen
check.explanation: There is no going back, no review screen and no penalty for guessing. A choice between two remaining options is a 50% chance; a blank is worth nothing.

sections.title: Budgeting 120 minutes
sections.body:
A countdown timer and an item counter stay on screen the whole time. The counter tells you how many items you have, but not how many of them are time burners, and a testlet or simlet counts as one item even though it holds several questions.

Use the rough rates from the Official Cert Guide: about **1 minute** for each multiple-choice or drag-and-drop item, and about **6 to 8 minutes** for each sim, simlet or testlet.

When the exam starts, do one subtraction. With N items and 120 minutes, the **slack** is 120 minus N: the extra time you have for time burners beyond a minute per item. If N is 100, the slack is about 20 minutes, enough for roughly three time burners at about 7 extra minutes each. Meet more than that and the regular items must go faster than a minute each.

To check your pace without doing much math, use Odom's time check: **expected minutes used = items answered + 7 for each time burner answered.** If you have answered 30 items, three of them simlets, you should have used about 30 + 21 = 51 minutes. Timer at 51: on pace. Well above: speed up. Below: you have slack.

Rules of thumb:

- Check your pace at a few fixed points (for example items 20, 40, 60 and 80), not after every question.
- Cap a regular item at about 2 or 3 minutes. Choose the best answer and move on; you cannot revisit it anyway.
- Do not rush the sims to bank time. There is no review pass to spend saved minutes on, and a sim is worth careful work.
- The timer does not stop for a restroom break, so take care of that before you start.

You get an erasable note board (or an on-screen whiteboard online). Many candidates spend the first minute writing a subnetting table so they never recompute it under pressure. Practice writing it before every Recurse practice exam so it takes less than a minute.
sections.code:
Time check: items answered + 7 per time burner

Items  Burners  Expected  Timer  Verdict
  20      1        27       25   2 min ahead
  45      3        66       74   8 min behind
  70      4        98       96   on pace

Slack at the start = 120 - number of items
  100 items -> 20 min for time burners
sections.tip: Recurse practice exams run 100 questions in 120 minutes. Note how much time you have left at the end of each one; finishing with under 10 minutes to spare means work on speed before you book.
sections.pitfall: Spending ten minutes on one hard multiple-choice item early on. That time comes out of the simulations at the end, which deserve the most care.

check.question: You have answered 40 items, 2 of them simlets, and the timer shows 62 minutes used. Using the time check (items + 7 per time burner), where are you?
choices: About 8 minutes ahead
Exactly on pace
22 minutes behind
About 8 minutes behind, so speed up on regular items
check.explanation: Expected time is 40 + 7 + 7 = 54 minutes. You have used 62, so you are about 8 minutes behind. Make firmer, faster choices on regular items; do not cut corners on the sims.

sections.title: Reading exhibits and eliminating answers
sections.body:
The author of the Official Cert Guide reports that instructors name the same top cause of wrong answers again and again: people do not read the question carefully enough. Screens train us to scan; exam items punish scanning. Use a fixed reading routine until it is automatic (adapted from Odom):

- **Step 1:** read the question stem fully, start to finish. Note exactly what it asks: which device, which direction, how many answers, and words like most likely, first and not.
- **Step 2:** scan the exhibit with that question in mind. Find the prompt (R1# or SW2#), the command that produced the output, and the lines that matter.
- **Step 3:** glance at the choices to see what kind of answer they are: commands, addresses, states, or statements.
- **Step 4:** reread the stem.
- **Step 5:** judge each choice against the exhibit as correct, definitely wrong, or maybe.

Know where to look in each common exhibit: the last two columns of show ip interface brief, Status and Duplex in show interfaces status, the three VLAN lists in show interfaces trunk, the longest matching prefix in show ip route, State in show ip ospf neighbor, and the lines and counters, top down, in show access-lists. The Troubleshooting and Show Commands topic in this path drills all of them.

Elimination raises your odds even when you are unsure. Strike choices that contradict the exhibit (an interface or VLAN that is not there), that use the wrong mode or syntax, or that are true statements answering a different question. For a choose-two item, judge each option on its own instead of hunting for a matching pair. Be wary of always and never in design or best-practice choices, but remember that protocol facts can be absolute.

Watch for the classic swaps: OSPF Neighbor ID versus neighbor address, CDP local Interface versus the neighbor's Port ID, NAT inside local versus inside global, a subnet ID offered as a host address, a wildcard offered as a subnet mask, and a configuration command offered in the wrong mode.
sections.code:
Q: Which TWO statements about SW1 are true?

SW1# show interfaces trunk

Port        Mode         Encapsulation  Status        Native vlan
Gi0/1       on           802.1q         trunking      99

Port        Vlans allowed on trunk
Gi0/1       10,20,99

Port        Vlans allowed and active in management domain
Gi0/1       10,99

Port        Vlans in spanning tree forwarding state and not pruned
Gi0/1       10,99

! Step 1: two answers, about SW1 only
! Step 2: one trunk, native VLAN 99, three lists
! Step 5: VLAN 20 is allowed but not active,
!         so it is missing or shut down on SW1
sections.tip: When an exhibit holds several commands, find the one the question is about first. Exhibits often include output that is accurate but irrelevant.
sections.pitfall: Answering from memory of a similar practice question instead of from this exhibit. Exam items change one detail (an address, a VLAN, a counter) to catch exactly that.

check.question: A choose-two item has five options. You are sure of one, and two others look equally plausible. What is the best approach?
choices: Judge each of the two against the exhibit on its own, then select exactly two in total
Select all three; the exam credits any correct one
Select only the one you are sure of
Pick the two options that sound most alike
check.explanation: The interface lets you select exactly the number asked for, and a guess is free. Rereading the stem and testing each remaining option against the exhibit usually separates them; if not, pick one rather than leaving the item short.

sections.title: Speed skills: subnetting and CLI fluency
sections.body:
Two skills decide whether you finish with time to spare: subnetting and moving around the CLI without thinking about it.

**Subnetting.** Many questions hide a subnetting step: is this gateway in the host's subnet, which route matches, which wildcard covers these hosts. The Official Cert Guide sets exam-ready goals of 100% accuracy at roughly these speeds, using only your head and the note board:

- Class, network ID and host count facts for an address: about 10 seconds.
- Converting a mask between dotted decimal, prefix and binary: about 15 seconds.
- Choosing the mask that meets a hosts-per-subnet requirement: about 15 seconds.
- Subnet ID, broadcast address and usable range for an address and mask: about 20 to 30 seconds.

Drill in short daily bursts (five minutes is plenty) rather than one long weekly session: spaced practice builds speed that lasts. Learn the magic number method, where the block size is 256 minus the mask value in the interesting octet, until you no longer convert to binary. The same table works in any octet, so a /20 is simply block 16 in the third octet. Wildcards are 255.255.255.255 minus the mask, and IPv6 compression (drop leading zeros, one :: for the longest run of zero groups) should be instant too.

**CLI fluency.** Sims and simlets test whether you know which mode a command lives in, which show command verifies each feature, and how to recover from a typo. Show commands run from privileged EXEC (add do in configuration mode), and many also work in user EXEC, which may be all a simlet gives you. Recurse's console labs grade exactly this: do every lab on the CCNA path at least twice, the second time without hints, and redo them when they come due.
sections.code:
Note board: write this in the first minute

Prefix  /25 /26 /27 /28 /29 /30
Mask    128 192 224 240 248 252
Block   128  64  32  16   8   4
Hosts   126  62  30  14   6   2

For /17 to /24 use the same row in the
third octet; for /9 to /16, the second.
sections.tip: Speed comes from not converting to binary. Memorize the mask values and block sizes; the magic number method then works entirely in decimal.
sections.pitfall: Drilling only easy last-octet masks. Exam items like /19, /21 and /22, where the interesting octet is the third; practice those until they feel the same.

activity.title: Beat the clock
activity.prompt: Run a timed drill. Before you book the exam, aim for five correct answers in a row at under 30 seconds each.

check.question: What is the subnet ID for 172.16.77.200/20?
check.explanation: A /20 mask is 255.255.240.0, so the block size is 16 in the third octet: 0, 16, 32, 48, 64, 80. The value 77 falls in the block starting at 64, giving 172.16.64.0.

sections.title: Booking, test-day rules and results
sections.body:
Booking takes three steps: create a Cisco account, sign in to Cisco's Certification Tracking System and complete your profile (this ties your exams to one candidate ID), then schedule and pay through Pearson VUE. Use your name exactly as it appears on your ID.

You choose between two delivery options. Read Pearson VUE's current Cisco rules before you choose, because the details change.

**Test center.** Cisco's policy requires two forms of ID, both with your signature, one of them a government-issued photo ID; the center also captures your photo and signature. Plan to arrive 15 to 30 minutes early. Everything personal, including your phone and watch, goes into a locker. You get an erasable note board or laminated sheet and a marker: ask for a spare marker and test both before you start.

**Online with OnVUE.** A live proctor watches you through your webcam. Run Pearson VUE's system test on the same computer and network you will use. You need a private, quiet room with a clear desk, a working webcam and microphone, and an accepted ID. Check-in starts shortly before the appointment and includes photos of your workspace taken with your phone, which then goes out of reach. During the exam, stay in view of the camera, do not talk or read aloud, and use no notes, phones or second screens; breaking the rules can end the attempt. Notes go on an on-screen whiteboard. A noisy household or an unreliable connection is a real risk, so a test center is the safer choice if your space is unpredictable.

Either way, you accept Cisco's confidentiality agreement before the first question. Sharing exam questions afterwards breaks it and can cost you the certification.

**Results** (check the current details on cisco.com). Cisco's policies say you receive a score report with a breakdown by exam section when you finish; the official result is the one recorded in the Certification Tracking System. If you pass, Cisco emails the next steps for your certificate and badge.

**Retakes and recertification** (verified on cisco.com in October 2026; check the current details on cisco.com). After a failed attempt you must wait five calendar days, counted from the day after the attempt, and pay again. The certification is valid for three years. You recertify before it expires by passing the exam again, by passing a higher-level Cisco exam, or by earning 30 Continuing Education credits. Cisco does not grant extensions.

sections.tip: Book a date four to six weeks out once practice scores reach the low 80s. A fixed date focuses the final weeks; check the reschedule deadline when you book in case you need to move it.
sections.pitfall: Assuming online testing is the easy option. Someone walking into the room, a second monitor left connected or a dropped connection can end the attempt.

check.question: What does Cisco's retake policy (at the time of writing) require after a failed CCNA attempt?
choices: Wait 30 days; the second attempt is free
Retake immediately at a reduced fee
Wait 180 days before retesting
Wait five calendar days, counted from the day after the attempt, and pay again
check.explanation: Cisco's published policy for associate exams is a five calendar day wait, starting the day after the failed attempt, at the normal price. The 180-day rule applies to retaking an exam you already passed.

sections.title: A 12-week plan with Recurse
sections.body:
About 140 hours of focused work takes most people from the basics to exam-ready: roughly 10 to 12 hours a week for 12 weeks. If you already work in networking, compress it. If you are new and busy, stretch it to 16 or 20 weeks rather than skipping the daily review.

Every study day has the same shape: clear your due review cards on Today first, then one new topic (lesson, section checks, activities), then its console lab, then a five-minute subnet drill. Each week also gets one Explain it (Feynman) session on the hardest topic of the week and one mixed quiz on everything studied so far, because mixing old and new topics is what keeps week 1 alive in week 12.

The weeks follow the CCNA path's stages:

- **Week 1:** networking basics, network components, cabling and interfaces, OSI with TCP and UDP. Lab: router bring-up.
- **Week 2:** IPv4 addressing and subnetting. The daily subnet drill starts here.
- **Week 3:** IPv6, Ethernet switching, wireless principles, virtualization and client IP settings. Lab: IPv6. Domain 1 quiz.
- **Week 4:** VLANs, trunking, CDP and LLDP, with their build and troubleshooting labs.
- **Week 5:** EtherChannel, spanning tree, wireless architectures, device management. Labs: EtherChannel, STP. Domain 2 quiz.
- **Week 6:** the routing table, static routing, inter-VLAN routing. Labs: static, floating static, IPv6 static, router-on-a-stick. Practice exam 1 as a baseline.
- **Week 7:** OSPF and first hop redundancy. Labs: OSPF, OSPF troubleshooting, HSRP. Domain 3 quiz.
- **Week 8:** NAT, DHCP and DNS, NTP, SNMP and syslog, QoS, SSH, TFTP and FTP, with their labs. Domain 4 quiz.
- **Week 9:** security concepts, device security, VPNs, ACLs, Layer 2 security. Labs: hardening, ACLs, port security, DHCP snooping.
- **Week 10:** wireless security and the WLC GUI, automation and SDN, REST APIs and JSON, Ansible and Terraform, AI and machine learning. Domain 5 and 6 quizzes. Practice exam 2.
- **Week 11:** Troubleshooting and Show Commands, every troubleshooting lab again, and your weakest domain from practice exam 2. Practice exam 3.
- **Week 12:** the final week (next section). Practice exam 4.

After every practice exam, study the topics behind each miss before the next one. The path's readiness score stays capped until you take a practice exam, because only a timed exam shows whether your knowledge holds up against the clock.
sections.code:
A study day (about 90 minutes)
20 min  Review: clear due cards on Today
35 min  New topic: lesson, checks, activities
25 min  Console lab for the topic
 5 min  Subnet drill
 5 min  Note one weak spot for the weekly quiz
sections.tip: If you fall behind, cut new material before you cut review. A skipped lesson costs a day; skipped review quietly erases weeks.
sections.pitfall: Saving every practice exam for the last week. A baseline in week 6 and weekly exams from week 10 leave time to fix what they reveal.

check.question: Midway through week 8 you have only 45 minutes for the day. What should you keep?
choices: Skip review and do the next lesson to stay on schedule
Clear your due review cards first, then use the rest on the current topic
Start a full 120-minute practice exam
Reread week 1's lessons from the start
check.explanation: Due cards are scheduled for just before you would forget them, so skipping them costs the most. New material can slip a day without losing anything already learned.

sections.title: The final week and exam day
sections.body:
The last week is for consolidation, not new topics.

- **Seven to four days out:** take a full timed practice exam under exam conditions: no notes, no Back button, phone in another room, only the note board you will really get. Review every miss and every lucky guess, then redo the labs for those topics. Confirm your ID, the appointment time, and your route or OnVUE setup.
- **Three to two days out:** a second practice exam if the first was under 85%. Otherwise, mixed quizzes on your weakest domain and a lap through the troubleshooting labs. Keep the daily review going.
- **The day before:** light review only: due cards, the subnet table, a few exhibits. Pack what you need (two IDs for a test center) and leave everything else at home. Then sleep. A clear head is worth more than one more fact, because most items test analysis, not recall.
- **Exam day:** eat, go easy on caffeine (the clock does not stop for restroom breaks), and arrive or check in early. Use the restroom before you start. In the first minute, write your subnet table. Read every stem fully, check your pace at fixed points, guess rather than leave anything blank, and answer every tab of a simlet before you click Next.
- **If you pass:** watch for Cisco's email about your certificate and badge, and note your three-year renewal date.
- **If you do not pass:** the hour right after the exam is your most valuable study hour. Write down every topic, command and concept that felt shaky (topics, never the questions themselves), compare them with your section scores, and plan a focused two to three week push before the retake.
sections.code:
Exam morning
[ ] ID checked, appointment time confirmed
[ ] Light breakfast, small coffee
[ ] Restroom before check-in
[ ] First minute: write the subnet table
[ ] Pace checks at items 20, 40, 60, 80
[ ] Every simlet tab answered before Next
sections.tip: Take at least one practice exam at the same time of day as your appointment, so your focus peaks when it counts.
sections.pitfall: Cramming new topics the night before. It raises anxiety, costs sleep and rarely adds a point; review what you already know instead.

check.question: What is the best use of the day before the exam?
choices: Learn a topic you skipped earlier
Take two back-to-back practice exams late into the night
Light review of due cards and the subnet table, then rest
Rewatch every lesson from week 1
check.explanation: Sleep and a calm, practiced routine help more than last-minute content. Light retrieval keeps things fresh without the fatigue of new material or long sessions.

lesson.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a friend who is booking a first CCNA attempt how the exam works, how to manage the clock and the one-way rule, and how to spend the final week before it.

questions.question: According to Cisco, how long is the CCNA 200-301 exam?
choices: 90 minutes
120 minutes
150 minutes
180 minutes
questions.explanation: Cisco's exam page lists a 120-minute duration (check the current details on cisco.com). Allow extra time on the day for check-in and the agreement screens.

questions.question: Which of these does Cisco publish for the 200-301 exam? (Choose three.)
choices: The exam duration
The exam price
The exam topics and their domain weights
The number of questions
The passing score
questions.explanation: Duration, price and the weighted exam topics are on cisco.com. Cisco does not publish the question count or the passing score, which is set statistically and can change.

questions.question: Match each CCNA domain to its weight in the exam topics.
questions.explanation: IP Connectivity (routing, OSPF, FHRP) is the heaviest at 25%. Network Access is also 20% and Automation and Programmability also 10%.

questions.question: An exam topic reads 'Describe the purpose, functions, and concepts of first hop redundancy protocols.' What does the verb tell you?
choices: Expect simulations that configure HSRP from scratch
Know the concepts well; configuration is not the focus
The topic is optional and rarely tested
Memorize every HSRP command and its options
questions.explanation: Describe and explain topics test concepts. Configure, verify and troubleshoot topics add commands and show output. You still need to recognize what HSRP output means, but deep configuration is not the target of that item.

questions.question: At the time of writing, what exam price in US dollars, before tax, did Cisco list for 200-301? (Prices change: check cisco.com.)
questions.explanation: Cisco listed USD 300 plus tax (also the price when the Official Cert Guide was printed). Local prices vary; Pearson VUE shows yours when you book.

questions.question: Match each exam item type to its description.

pairs.right: One scenario with several multiple-choice questions
A simulated network you explore with show commands, then answer questions
A simulated network you configure or fix
Match or order items by moving them
Square check boxes and a stated number to choose

questions.explanation: Simlets test verification (reading state); simulations test configuration (changing it). Testlets look like simlets without the live devices.

questions.question: On the CCNA exam, can you return to a standalone question after clicking Next?
choices: Yes, from a review screen shown at the end of the exam
Yes, as long as you flagged it before moving on
Only during the last 10 minutes of the exam
No; it locks when you move on and there is no review screen
questions.explanation: Cisco exams are one-way. Answer each item as if it were the last time you will see it, because it is.

questions.question: In a simlet with four tabs, you have answered three and click Next. What happens?
choices: The exam blocks you until all four tabs are answered
The unanswered tab is carried to the end of the exam for review
A generic prompt asks whether to move on, without saying a tab is blank; the blank tab earns nothing
The fourth tab is skipped and does not count
questions.explanation: Inside a simlet or testlet you can move between tabs, but the exit prompt does not flag an unanswered tab or too few selections. Check every tab before you leave the scenario.

questions.question: You cannot work out a multiple-choice question. What is the best action?
choices: Eliminate what you can and choose an answer; there is no guessing penalty
Leave it blank, because wrong answers cost points
Flag it and return to it at the end
Skip it, since unanswered items are not scored
questions.explanation: A blank and a wrong answer both earn nothing, and there is no going back, so an educated guess can only help.

questions.question: A simlet gives you only user EXEC access (R1>). Which command will NOT work?
choices: show running-config
show ip interface brief
show ip route
show cdp neighbors
questions.explanation: show running-config needs privileged EXEC. Many verification commands work at R1>, so learn to answer from show ip interface, show ip route, show ip protocols and similar output.

questions.question: How does the exam software handle multiple-answer questions? (Choose two.)
choices: It states how many answers to choose
It stops you selecting more than that number
It shows the options with round radio buttons
It lets you revisit the question after you click Next
It deducts points for each wrong selection
questions.explanation: Multiple-answer items use square check boxes, state the number to pick, block extra selections and warn about too few. There is no guessing penalty and no revisiting.

questions.question: Using the time check (items answered + 7 per time burner), how many minutes should you have used after 25 items that include 2 simlets?
questions.explanation: 25 items + 7 + 7 for the two simlets = 39 minutes. Compare that with the timer to see whether you are ahead or behind.

questions.question: The item counter shows 104 items. How much slack do you have for time burners beyond a pace of 1 minute per item?
choices: About 104 minutes
None; every item gets exactly 1 minute
About 16 minutes, enough for roughly two time burners
About 60 minutes
questions.explanation: 120 - 104 = 16 minutes of slack. A time burner takes about 6 to 8 minutes, roughly 6 or 7 more than a regular item, so 16 minutes covers about two. More burners mean regular items must go faster.

questions.question: How does the exam's item counter count a testlet that contains four questions?
choices: As four items
As one item
As two items
It is not counted
questions.explanation: A testlet or simlet counts as one item, which is why they make the counter a poor guide to remaining time.

questions.question: At item 60 you are about 15 minutes behind your time check. What is the best response?
choices: Submit the remaining simulations blank to save time
Rush through the simulations to bank time for review
Stop checking the clock so it does not distract you
Make firmer, faster choices on regular items and keep full effort for the sims
questions.explanation: Regular items are where time is recovered: cap them at a minute or two. Sims are worth careful work, there is no review pass to bank time for, and blank sims throw away points.

questions.question: Put the question-reading routine adapted from the Official Cert Guide in order.
items: Scan the exhibit with the question in mind
Glance at the choices to see what type of answer they are
Judge each choice against the exhibit
questions.explanation: Reading the stem first tells you what to look for in the exhibit. The second read catches qualifiers such as not, first and most likely before you commit.

questions.question: Which two statements about SW1 are true? (Choose two.)
questions.code:
SW1# show interfaces trunk

Port        Mode         Encapsulation  Status        Native vlan
Gi0/1       on           802.1q         trunking      99

Port        Vlans allowed on trunk
Gi0/1       10,20,99

Port        Vlans allowed and active in management domain
Gi0/1       10,99

Port        Vlans in spanning tree forwarding state and not pruned
Gi0/1       10,99
choices: VLAN 20 is allowed on the trunk but not active on SW1
The native VLAN on Gi0/1 is 99
Spanning tree is blocking VLAN 20 on Gi0/1
Gi0/1 is not trunking
VLAN 10 is not allowed on the trunk
questions.explanation: VLAN 20 is in the first list but missing from the second, so it is not defined or is shut down on SW1; STP blocking would remove it only from the third list. The native VLAN column shows 99, and Status shows trunking.

questions.question: Match each exhibit field or situation to the correct reading.

pairs.right: The neighbor's router ID, not its interface address
Your local port, not the neighbor's
The inside host's address as seen outside
Matches a /24 range; it is not a subnet mask

pairs.left: A port missing from show vlan brief
pairs.right: Possibly a trunk, which that command never lists

questions.explanation: Exam distractors often swap exactly these pairs. Knowing which side of each pair a field shows saves time and points.

questions.question: Which answer choice can you eliminate first in a question about R2's exhibit?
choices: One that names an interface missing from R2's output
One that uses a qualifier such as most or usually
The longest choice, since correct answers are short
One that recommends a show command to verify
questions.explanation: A choice that contradicts the exhibit, such as an interface or VLAN that is not there, is wrong whatever else it says. Length or wording alone proves nothing.

questions.question: What is the broadcast address of the subnet containing 10.20.37.130/26?
questions.explanation: /26 has a block size of 64 in the last octet: 0, 64, 128, 192. 130 is in the 128 block, so the subnet is 10.20.37.128 and the broadcast is 128 + 64 - 1 = 191.

questions.question: What is the subnet ID for 172.30.150.10/21?
questions.explanation: /21 is 255.255.248.0, a block of 8 in the third octet: ..., 136, 144, 152. 150 falls in the 144 block, so the subnet ID is 172.30.144.0.

questions.question: Which dotted-decimal mask is /27?
questions.explanation: /27 borrows 3 bits in the last octet: 128 + 64 + 32 = 224. /26 is 192, /28 is 240 and /29 is 248.

questions.question: What exam-ready speed does the Official Cert Guide set for finding the subnet ID, broadcast and usable range of an address?
choices: About 2 minutes
Any speed, as long as it is accurate
Under 5 seconds
About 20 to 30 seconds, with 100% accuracy
questions.explanation: Any speed is fine while learning, but the exam-ready goal is 100% accuracy in about 20 to 30 seconds, with simpler tasks such as mask conversion in about 15.

questions.question: How many usable host addresses does a /28 subnet provide?
questions.explanation: A /28 leaves 4 host bits: 2^4 = 16 addresses, minus the subnet ID and broadcast, gives 14 usable hosts.

questions.question: What wildcard mask matches the same range as the subnet mask 255.255.240.0?
What identification does Cisco's policy require at a Pearson VUE test center?
choices: Any one photo ID, such as a student card
Two IDs with your signature, one a government photo ID
Your Cisco candidate ID and a credit card
The confirmation email from Pearson VUE
questions.explanation: Cisco's exam policies require two IDs bearing your signature, one of them a government-issued photo ID, plus a digital photo and signature taken at check-in. Check Pearson VUE's current rules for your country.

questions.question: Which are typical rules for taking a Cisco exam online with OnVUE? (Choose three.)
choices: Run the system test on the exam computer and network beforehand
Test alone in a private room with a clear desk
Stay in view of the webcam for the whole exam
Keep printed notes within reach if you show them to the proctor
Take a scheduled 10-minute break at the halfway point
questions.explanation: OnVUE needs a working setup, a private, clear workspace and continuous monitoring. Printed notes are not allowed and there is no scheduled break. Check Pearson VUE's current Cisco rules before booking.

questions.question: Under Cisco's retake policy at the time of writing, how many calendar days must you wait after a failed CCNA attempt before retesting?
questions.explanation: Five calendar days, counted from the day after the failed attempt (check the current details on cisco.com).

questions.question: For how long is a CCNA certification valid before you must recertify?
choices: One year
Two years
Three years
For life
questions.explanation: Associate certifications are valid for three years. Cisco sends reminders, but recertifying on time is your responsibility.

questions.question: Which actions recertify an active CCNA before it expires? (Choose two; check the current details on cisco.com.)
choices: Pass the current CCNA exam again
Earn 30 Continuing Education credits
Pay a renewal fee within a grace period after it expires
Pass an entry-level CCST exam
Log 100 hours of lab practice
questions.explanation: Cisco lists retaking the exam, passing a higher-level exam, or earning 30 CE credits for associate certifications. There is no grace period or extension, and a lower-level exam does not renew a CCNA.

questions.question: After the exam you plan to post the questions you remember for a study group. What is the problem?
choices: Nothing, as long as you do not share the answers
It is allowed once you have passed the exam
Only the simulations are covered by confidentiality
It breaks Cisco's confidentiality agreement
questions.explanation: Every candidate accepts Cisco's confidentiality agreement before the first question. Sharing exam content can lead to revoked certifications and bans. Note shaky topics for yourself instead.

questions.question: Put the steps for taking your first Cisco exam in order.
items: Complete your profile in the Certification Tracking System
Schedule and pay through Pearson VUE
Run the OnVUE system test or plan your route to the center
Sit the exam and check the result in the Certification Tracking System
questions.explanation: The Cisco account and tracking profile come first, because they tie the exam to your candidate record; Pearson VUE handles scheduling, payment and delivery.

questions.question: In the 12-week plan, what comes first in every study session?
choices: A new lesson for the week's topic
A timed practice exam
Clearing due review cards on Today
A console lab for the current topic
questions.explanation: Due cards are timed for just before you would forget them. Doing them first protects everything already learned, and the new topic follows.

questions.question: Why take a practice exam at the end of week 6, when half the topics are still untaught?
choices: To learn the format and pace early and see which completed domains are weak
To decide whether to skip the remaining topics
Because the score at week 6 predicts the real result
Because Recurse locks later lessons until you do
questions.explanation: An early baseline makes the format and clock familiar and shows weak spots in domains 1 and 2 while there is time to fix them. The score itself is expected to be low.

questions.question: Put the CCNA domains in the order the Recurse path teaches them.
questions.explanation: The path follows Cisco's numbering, which also builds on itself: addressing and switching before VLANs, VLANs before routing between them, routing before NAT, ACLs and automation.

questions.question: Your last three practice exams scored 78%, 81% and 79%, and your exam is in 10 days. What is the best move?
choices: Sit the exam as booked, since 80% is surely a pass
Retake the same practice exam until you remember it
Stop review and reread every lesson from the start
Drill the weakest domains and reschedule if scores stay under 85%
questions.explanation: Nobody outside Cisco knows the passing score, and scores near 80% leave no margin. Targeted work on weak domains, checked with fresh practice exams, is the fastest way up; memorizing a repeated exam inflates the score without adding skill.

questions.question: What is a good use of the first minute of the exam?
choices: Write your subnetting table on the note board
Skim ahead to see the simulations
Answer the easiest questions first
Read the confidentiality agreement again
questions.explanation: A practiced subnet table saves time on every subnetting item. You cannot skim ahead or reorder questions, because the exam is one-way.

questions.question: Which belong in the final week before the exam? (Choose three.)
choices: A full timed practice exam under exam conditions
Redoing the labs for topics you missed
Keeping the daily review going
Starting a topic you have not studied yet
Staying up late to cram the night before
questions.explanation: The final week consolidates: realistic practice, fixing gaps found by that practice, and continued review. New topics and lost sleep both cost more than they add.

questions.question: Why should you limit caffeine and use the restroom right before the exam?
choices: Test centers do not allow drinks in the building
The exam clock keeps running during a break
Caffeine is banned by the confidentiality agreement
Breaks are only allowed after item 50
questions.explanation: The timer does not stop if you leave the room, and leaving also takes time with the staff. Online, leaving the camera view can end the attempt.

questions.question: You did not pass. What is the most useful thing to do in the next hour?
choices: Post the questions you remember to a forum and ask for answers
Write down every topic, command and concept that felt shaky, without recording the questions
Book the retake for the next morning
Restart the 12-week plan from week 1
questions.explanation: Memory of what confused you fades fast, so capture topics right away and match them to your section scores. Posting questions breaks the confidentiality agreement, and a next-day retake is not allowed or wise.
